speechtext:

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERS' SESSIONAL AND EXPENSE ALLOWANCES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret that my remarks are being accompanied at this point with such a great deal of hilarity because I am speaking, on a very serious matter. In introducing this amendment, which deals with the date on which this act shall come into force, I am really contemplating delaying the coming into effect of any increase in indemnity until after the date of the next general election. I fully appreciate that many members from distant ridings have in the past experienced, and are currently experiencing, some financial difficulty with the present indemnities and allowances. The financial objectives, of course, are recognized, especially the one that requires two residences, one in the riding of the member concerned and another in Ottawa. Similarly, the need for additional transportation expenses is both real and legitimate. The Beaupre report had some comments to make upon at least one of those two items, but the government has not seen fit to accept the recommendations of its own commission in this regard, and this I regret.
A greater expense burden is placed on those members who represent ridings which are geographically isolated, extremely widespread or scattered than the burden on those who represent relatively compact or nearby ridings such as those in Ottawa, Montreal and the Toronto area. The cost of an additional residence and an addition car represents a sizeable drain on the financial resources of any Member of Parliament, particularly those coming from the far east or the far west, or those representing rural or northern ridings.
I can appreciate the fact that those members who are in favour of an immediate pay raise might well be moved to ask why, in view of my remarks, I do not vote for the raise. My answer to this hypothetical and rhetorical question is that I have no philosophical objection to a pay raise for MP's or anybody else, but I do object to the size of the raise and its timing. I personally resent being put in the unacceptable position of voting myself a pay hike, and I will try to be more specific in that respect as I continue my remarks. I am also disappointed that the Beaupre report recommendations were not followed to assist those people representing ridings which require

June 1, 1971

greater financial demands because of their remoteness as compared to compact ridings near the urban centres.
No one can really win by taking part in this debate on this issue because if you are in favour of the increase you are considered to be greedy and irresponsible, and if you vote against the raise you are considered to be a hypocrite who secretly wants the money but wants to gain the political advantage of opposing such an increase. I suggest that view is widely held not only by some people in this House but also by members of the general public.
I have no objection to voting for a reasonable raise for the position of a Member of Parliament or for extra expenses, facilities or the staff necessary for a member to perform his job more adequately. It is for this reason I put my amendment forward. This is precisely why I feel any increase in salary or expenses should not come into force immediately but following the next general election. Under those circumstances, I would then be voting for an increase in salary for the position rather than for myself. There is little guarantee that anyone who is a member of this Parliament will be sitting as a member of the next Parliament.
I am prepared to vote for the upgrading of the position of a Member of Parliament. This position should be recognized by a salary increase. I am in favour of that if it can be handled in a different manner. Perhaps it should be tied to some salary scale in the civil service, or some other formula. This is not the case now. One of the main reasons for putting forward this amendment is the fact that this is our last hope of modifying the government proposal put forward at the worst possible time. I resent being put in the position of having to deal with this issue in the manner in which I am forced to do. Having been here for some three years, I am satisfied that the duties and financial responsibilities of an MP demand a constant reappraisal of financial return. No one comes here to make money. Most members are rewarded less than they would receive from their private occupations outside this place. However, I do not believe that Parliament should be the private preserve of those people with sufficient substance or wealth so that the size of an MP's indemnity is irrelevant. Parliament can be, should be and is to a large extent a reflection of various groups of Canadian society. The financial rewards, then must be such that the average Joe can run for office and serve his time here without taking a financial shellacking, therefore, there is a real need for constant reappraisal of the indemnity and expenses of MP's.
While the Beaupre did not propose a formula, it at least indicated the direction in which we should travel. The House leader has attempted to get the various parties to come together on a formula but I am sorry his negotiations failed. I am in favour of a pay increase coming into force only after the next election. While my expenses are much greater than I anticipated before I was a member-I admit that I did not fully understand the nature of the job or the demands placed upon a member-I emphasize that that dilemma is not unique in respect of the office of MP. All groups and societies have experienced inflation and the consequent reduction of the
Senate and House of Commons Act
value of our dollar in real terms. If there is anything unique about the position of an MP, it is that he is a member of one of the few groups in society which can vote itself a raise in pay.
Other groups, which perhaps need an increase urgently, must depend on others to vote for that increase. Most have to go through elaborate bargaining processes. We do not have to do this. The timing of this raise is particularly inopportune in view of the government's proposed two-year period of restraint in other segments of our society. Perhaps after the next general election the economic conditions of the country will be different. I have not much faith in that line of argument, but I put it forward to indicate that the general public is quite critical of this proposed increase. There is a vast number of adults and students who are unemployed. The contemplated change proposed for our financial status does not automatically assure a similar prospect for the thousands of unemployed people. They cannot improve their status as we can. Someone else must do it for them.
When I ran for office 1 was a big boy, and I knew what I was doing.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT

speechtext: What happened, did you shrink?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERS' SESSIONAL AND EXPENSE ALLOWANCES. ETC.
speechtext:
I am sure some members think that I have shrunk since but I consider the personal rewards of a session of Parliament to be part of what I view as a contractual obligation. No matter how it hurts, members should be content with the $12,000 and $6,000 for the life of this Parliament. I am certain I will not receive substantial agreement on this point. I believe MP's salaries should be related to those of others on fixed income, veterans and pensioners, subject to yearly revision on the basis of a formula. We should try to avoid this controversy which occurs when we allow our salaries to remain in status quo for a period of 10 years and then propose a substantial hike. The government House leader has tried to explain that this increase is not a substantial hike but represents only five per cent or six per cent per year to bring our salary level up to date. The general public considers it a substantial hike, however, as compared to the increases the average individual is receiving. They feel this increase is substantial, monstrous and irresponsible.
I note that the government has abandoned, however, any attempt to reflect the cost of living in the old age security pension. We abandoned this last fall. A great number of people regret that even the limited two per cent escalator has been abandoned which was designed to perhaps bring some protection into old age security at a time when the value of our dollar was shrinking because of inflation at the rate of approximately five per cent per year.
Next, I should like the position of Member of Parliament to be recognized for salary purposes, rather than the person. In this way, during the next election citizens would have an opportunity in the ridings to choose from between three of four members who they would like to

June 1, 1971
Senate and House of Commons Act
see occupy the particular position. I believe this improvement in social justice would be accomplished by the passage of my amendment. The people would have an opportunity to decide which of three or four persons is the most worthy. Any political gain or disadvantage would then not accrue to anyone regardless of his vote today on this issue. I believe, by supporting my amendment, we would be recognizing the need for an increase but would be divorcing it from the individual member. This is what I would prefer.
Earlier, I expressed my regret that the government apparently had tossed aside the Beaupre Commission report. I know the government House leader said that the individual Member of Parliament could decide to do the things the Beaupre Commission recommended. I am not sure all the things the Beaupre Commission recommended could be accomplished by the individual member but certainly some could. Better research, office facilities and vouchered expenses reflecting riding needs have all been virtually ignored, so each member now is left with the decision, according to his own conscience, whether he wishes to use the money for the purposes suggested by the Beaupre Commission or pocket the increase himself.
I shall close by urging members to vote in favour of the amendment because it seems to me that only by supporting it can we at once recognize the need for a reasonable and responsible indemnity for Members of Parliament, with adjustments from time to time and also some better permanent legislation on this important matter.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to mention anything that happened during the question period, but I am glad the gremlins have not decided to inhibit this desk. What I started to say before my dulcet tones could be carried across the chamber was that I confess what I am about to say may not appear to be too logical, and I admit readily that this is so, to those who heard what I had to say when this bill first came before the House. Hon. members will think I should support the amendment advanced by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose). I do not. I do not question the sincerity of the hon. member. Obviously, we cannot do that and it is a good thing that we cannot do it. I would
not do so in this case in any event, because the hon. member is a personal friend of mine.
When I spoke earlier I felt very seriously that a pay increase, separate from an allowance for expenses, was not justified for a number of reasons which I shall not repeat now. I also said that such a pay increase should come after the election. The hon. member's amendment, however, would put the whole problem over until after the election. There is not a member in any seat in the House of Commons, including the hon. member, who does not know that expenses, allowances and out-of-pocket money with which members are involved week in and week out needs readjustment, reassessment and revision. It is for that reason the hon. member's amendment goes too far.
I considered moving an amendment to eliminate that part of the bill referring to salary increases. I, personally, deliberated the question and felt, perhaps wrongly, that it was not up to me to put individual members on the spot in respect of such a sensitive issue which affects all of us. This is why, although in my earlier speech I said I would endeavour to see if an amendment could be developed, I confess I did nothing during the committee proceedings even if I could have. Also I do not have a formal amendment to move today which would enable members to pick and choose, thus putting them on the spot in respect of expenses and salary. In my opinion, members, no matter how maligned they are from all sources, be it from the editorials, cartoons and people who write letters to the editor, do need a review and adjustment of their expenses and allowances. That is why I give full credit to the President of the Privy Council, the government House leader, for attempting

and at one time I was most optimistic there would be some success in his attempt-to have included in this bill a provision for a regular review and revision of salaries so that members would not again be confronted with the invidious practice of having to speak for or against the amount that goes into their pocketbooks.
It makes me sad that the President of the Privy Council was not able to get an all-party agreement to amend the bill. It was thus a surprise to me that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) withdrew his amendment which, in effect, would go part way in providing for a permanent review porcedure which would obviate the necessity of members going through this moment of truth in making a decision which affects their pocketbooks. Such decisions can be misinterpreted or interpreted in any way one wishes. However, I am not supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West. I also cannot support this bill. The bill which the hon. member attempts to amend, I believe, is a bad bill at this time. My main objection is that I believe it destroys the credibility of this institution as it relates to any economic matters involving restraint, discipline or control. One does not have to be a soothsayer to know that Parliament, in the months ahead, will be confronted from time to time with economic problems and with the duty of preaching the philosophy of restraint, discipline and control.

June 1, 1971

Furthermore, I believe, and I could make a speech on this topic alone, that this bill at this time downgrades Parliament in the eyes of the public. I said previously that I would not accept any benefits from this bill. Well, I went too far, and I admit it. An hon. member from behind the curtains says he wants them now. I also want them. If the hon. member behind the curtain comes to his seat-and I know who he is but I will not challenge him-I will show him that I never spoke against the principle of a review and a substantial upward revision in expenses and allowances of members. I also admitted freely that members needed an increase. So, my position, over which the hon. member behind the curtain chuckles, is one that I am prepared to face because it looks as though I have done a flip flop. In reality, however, it is no different from the one I took when I made my speech previously. But in honour to my friend behind the curtain I not only revise what I said, I repent in part for what I said.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERS' SESSIONAL AND EXPENSE ALLOWANCES. ETC.
speechtext:
There is no doubt in my mind, as I said previously, that members need an increase in funds for living expenses. Many have attacked this bill in a most negative fashion and some have mouthed platitudes against the bill, but nevertheless admit they will accept the fruits of the subject of their attack in whatever form or fashion. Some say they will donate the amount of the increase to charity. I must say that I explored this possibility but found there are more than mechanical difficulties. There are monetary difficulties in being Santa Claus to so many deserving Canadians. Of those who say they would donate it to charity, some may be able to afford it. I admit I cannot. Some members say they will be Pied Pipers in their ridings, dispensing dollars for charitable projects. Let them go to it. I cannot and I will not be a part of such hypocrisy. Some members say they will set up offices in their riding. Fine; let them go ahead, but once they do they will be accepting the bounty of this bill. Let us not fool ourselves. If they accept the bounty of the bill, then those members should not rail so aggressively against it.
To put it simply, I believe honestly that my instincts are right, but my pocketbook cannot afford them. Therefore, I intend to take the increase, and thus I feel I cannot vote against the bill. But since I believe so fundamentally in what I said earlier about the bill and its negative character, I cannot support the bill. Therefore I find myself in a sterile, neuter and, in effect, negative position for the first time in my life as a member and so will deliberately abstain from voting on this bill. This is why I am making this short speech.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MEMBERS' SESSIONAL AND EXPENSE ALLOWANCES. ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to miss the opportunity to state my views on the bill now under consideration, since I feel it is quite important. Some hon. members have been putting on a big show since the bill was introduced. I will not have anything to
Senate and House of Commons Act
do with that and I would like to say immediately that I welcome this bill.
I think that a member has some heavy responsibilities. Some object to the bill claiming that its passage would be untimely. It was the same in 1968 when I was elected. It was too soon then to deal with an increase of our parliamentary salary. It was again too soon in 1969. However now it is too late because I imagine that an election will be called within a year and then, the passage of the bill will have to be delayed till 1972 or 1973.
Mr. Speaker, some hon. members are putting on a big show since they don't need an increase. They should, at least, have the decency to allow those who need it to use this additional income provided by this increase. On the other hand, there are those who extol virtue, but are not prepared to practise it. They should be honest enough to admit it.
Mr. Speaker, two election campaigns have just ended where odious comparisons have been made between the increase of 42 cents granted to some disabled people and veterans and this increase of $8,000 for Members of Parliament. Of course, this made for an interesting debate for the people to listen to. On the one hand, some hon. members blamed the government for introducing this bill and on the other, some considered this increase insufficient.
I believe the opposition parties blamed the government for that truly insufficient increase. There can be no comparison between that last one and the present proposal. Electionwise, that was interesting and perhaps profitable.
Through arousal of feelings of all kinds, there is again today an attempt to gain politically from this increase. It might be interesting to know who is against the increase and who is afraid, for instance, of seeing Parliament lose some of its prestige. As for myself, I am wondering how much a member of Parliament is worth.
I made a few studies recently and I calculated how many hours members of Parliament put in-because most of them work hard-and I arrived at the figure of $3.46 per hour. Of course, I must include the hours I spend at my office on weekends. I think that I am not the only one in this House to do so much overtime on weekends.
On several occasions, I had the opportunity to ask some ladies how much their husbands were earning. The answer was $4 or $5 an hour, in the case of professionals. I came to the conclusion that $3.46 was not exaggerated if we take into account the responsibilities inherent to the position of Member of Parliament.
I am convinced that several hon. members do know that the salary increase will be passed. I am one of those who look forward to it, and I do not hesitate in saying that this has become highly necessary in view of the responsibilities involved in my work. It is true that during the election campaign of 1968, I agreed to serve in this Parliament for the current salary. However, it was difficult for me, at that time, to know what amount of work this position implied. In the light of my experience so far, I quite agree now with the proposal of the govern-

ment. I blame it for one thing only: that it waited until today to have this House vote on it!
I feel that my opinion reflects the views of the majority, and I would invite hon. members, if they want to be honest with the population as they would like to be, at least to undertake to give this raise to charities if they think they do not need it and that this legislation is unacceptable.
I would like to be able to afford handing over that increase to charitable organizations. But I am not, Mr. Speaker. I shall use it simply to meet my present obligations.
I shall dwell on the matter no longer, but I had to express my views. I wanted to ask those who are against that increase to make less of a political issue of it or commit themselves officially to handing it over to charitable institutions. I know that, in my riding, the St. Vincent of Paul Society would be only too happy if I were to hand over the $8,000 a year. And I would be happy to do so, but I cannot afford it. The majority of members, except for those who are wealthy, cannot do any thing else but follow suit; but those who make political hay of the issue and oppose the bill in order to be able to say during the election campaign that they were against it, even though they accepted it, will be judged by the people.
I wanted to make these few remarks to ask other members who could be tempted to go on electioneering on this subject to refrain from doing so in order that we could now proceed to the vote; I will thus be in a position to take advantage of this raise to provide better service to my constituents and a better response to all solicitations for an improved administration of my constituency and I will also be better armed to defend the interests of my people.
It is with this in mind that I will welcome the raise and I am grateful to the government for acknowledging that you need money to go into politics and that I am not especially fond of having to work under difficult conditions. It is difficult for most people to accept and to understand the proper role of MP's and the expenses it entails. It is hard to understand that we should experience difficulty in getting along with our salary, but should we have to explain in minute details that our job involves some obligations and in this regard, I will refer to the invitations we receive from the public.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, I hope this raise will not be delayed any longer and our situation should not prevent us from understanding that other groups of citizens also need higher incomes; furthermore, I do not hesitate in supporting the groups of citizens who are now in need of salary increases. I am not aware of this and I agree with it.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STAMP AGENTS' COMMISSION, LETTER MAIL PREPARATION ARRANGEMENTS, EXTRAORDINARY SERVICES, MEMBERS' MAIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time now the postal department has indicated that the only category of mail which constantly pays its own way is first class mail, yet we note that the full impact of this increase with fall on those who use first class mail. This increase is from six cents to seven cents per letter on July 1, and from seven cents to eight cents on January 1, 1972. Within the last three years we have seen an increase in the rates for first class mail from four cents to eight cents, including letters posted for delivery in local areas. Thus the increase on January 1 of next year will be 100 per cent.
The time has arrived to look at the source of the revenue of the postal department. We must make some concessions on behalf of those people who are paying for the greatly reduced and inferior postal service. Only five years ago when you mailed a letter in a community for
[Mr. Gray.)
June 1, 1971

delivery in that area it cost lour cents. At that time such a letter would have been delivered the same day as a result of a twice-daily delivery service. After January 1 of this coming year, we will be required to place an eight cent stamp on a letter for delivery in a local community. We will have once-a-day delivery, so if the letter is not posted in time it will be delivered perhaps two days later, if you are lucky. Not only is there this built-in delay, but we find that the cost of the service and the efficiency have increased and decreased respectively. As a result of the new service, it will take four or five days to deliver a letter within a community.
I have heard stories, as I am sure other hon. members have, about what happens when someone is at the end of a postal walk. When there are letters that have not been delivered at the end of a postal walk they are taken back and put in the box again. If there should be too much mail again on the second day, the same mail might be taken back a second time. If a person lives close to the end of a postal walk or at a point where the postal employee might be at the time he goes home or leaves for lunch, that person might wait from Monday until Wednesday to have his mail delivered. The minister in charge of the post office should be prepared to say why he believes first class mail should carry the major share of the cost of the mail service in this country. He has said he will have mail delivered across Canada at a much accelerated rate. He made some suggestions, but he has not been able to produce. There are many instances in which mail service in Canada is not as fast today as it was.
There is no question but that in Northern Ontario 20 years ago mail was delivered at least one or two days sooner, on an average, than it is now. Occasionally, a letter mailed in Toronto is received in Northern Ontario the next morning, but this must be the result of an accident in which the letter got mixed up in some way and managed to get there. There was a time when if you mailed a letter before four o'clock in the afternoon in Toronto, it would be placed in the box in New Liskeard, 400 miles away, between four o'clock and eight o'clock in the morning. This variation in time was caused by the variation in the time of arrival of the train; it was never on time. However, that letter was always there the next day. All business in northern Ontario was based on a one-day delivery service in that area. Better than that, if you posted a letter in the postal box at any railway station or handed it to the man on the train as it went by, the letter would be dropped off at any delivery point along that railway line. Now, if a letter is put in the mail box at the station it will probably be taken back to the post office because it will go out on a bus.
Obviously, mail cannot be sorted en route in a bus. That was tried in the United States. They used a gyro car which is a truck with the body suspended to compensate for the movement. They found they could not keep people at that type of work. It has been impossible to have sorting en route. This means that in northern
Post Office Act
Ontario the mail has to be sent to a distributing point. The mail goes to the post office and is handled through the sorting system. It is then sent to a distribution point for delivery. If there is insufficient time to do the sorting at the first distribution point, it is put back into the box and sent to another distribution point at the other end of the line. I understand this is how the mail is handled now that road transportation is used. So, I sympathize with the minister in charge of the post office.
There does not seem to be any way, because of the manner in which the mail is presently handled, to have decent service. If the service is reduced, then the cost also, to some extent, must be reduced because there no longer is sorting in cars on the railways. The people who rode in those cars year after year are no longer employed in that position. The mail at a distribution point is handled through the normal sorting procedure and, therefore, there probably is a reduction in the cost of handling that mail.
I presume the reason the government dropped the mail contract with the Ontario Northland Railway was that it was very expensive. So, expenses are being reduced. To my knowledge no one in this House who represents a riding, urban or rural, would say that we are getting better service now than we did 20 years ago. Twenty years ago letters were delivered for 3 cents. Now, on January 1, the rate is to be 8 cents. The former Postmaster General said he would do something about this problem. He sure did. He got things into such a state that the employees were walking up and down in front of the Parliament buildings almost every day a year after they had a disagreement with the Post Office Department. The minister has not been able to tell them that the government has nothing to say to them because every few months or so another suggestion is made to these employees. They are given another offer which they can negotiate. Nothing has been solved. The result of all the negotiations has been dissatisfaction and disillusionment with the Post Office Department. This has created very low morale and a very poor relationship between the public and the postal employees. It has resulted in the public being dissatisfied with the type of service they receive.
If the rate for first class mail is to be raised from 6 cents to 7 cents and then increased to eight cents by January, why is the minister not in a position to say we are now able to have mail delivered twice a day. Why is he not able to say that the problem of the delay in many areas has been solved, and that the postal service will meet the standard that we established 20 years ago. I am not referring to a standard that we should have in the future but rather the standard we had 20 years ago. A large proportion of the cost of the postal department is being paid by the revenue from first class mail. I suggest we should be told if we are receiving some other benefits for the expenditure we are making.
The minister has not indicated that there will be any relief for the social, charitable, religious, labour and trade magazines. These magazines were very important

June 1, 1971
Post Office Act
to the economy of our nation. Most of the farmers we talk to today still lament the fact that most of the farm publications have gone out of business as a result of the attitude of this government toward postal rates. The government has not done a damn thing about such magazines as Time and Reader's Digest. We understand that the same subsidization is being paid by the post office to Time and Reader's Digest that was originally negotiated. Neither Reader's Digest nor Time magazine, for all their comments, have done anything but provide Canadians with a lower cost propaganda machine, and most of the reports that we see in those magazines that are published in Canada have a slant in line with that in the parent magazine. But if the general public, the people who drop a letter in the mail box, are going to subsidize the reading material of this nation, then I suggest they could use their money to better advantage by subsidizing those magazines that were dropped as well as some of the trade publications that were beneficial to large segments of our population.
Much of the development in the agricultural field was brought to the attention of the farmers and of the entrepreneurs in the agricultural sphere by the articles that appeared in those magazines. I never found many people in Canada who were interested in providing such subsidization as we are now giving to Reader's Digest and Time magazine, but I have found many Canadians who would have preferred the government to subsidize magazines for the rural communities. They were one of the major instruments for social development in that segment of the population and helped to develop our rural way of life.
I did mention the fact that we have not done much to improve the relationship of the employees with the Post Office. Morale among post office employees in my area has had its ups and downs. In the last year or two, I have received numerous complaints about employees of the post office and about the fact that they do not seem to be very interested in serving the customer. They have a certain job to do at a certain time and that is all they care about. Customers can line up and wait or do whatever they want. The relationship of the employees to their customers is not as friendly as it used to be three or four years ago when people dropped into the post office for a kind of social gathering. They met there in the morning to exchange the news of the day. The rapport at present is not nearly as good as it used to be several years ago.
Why is there no indication in the bill of the view of the government as to whether it wants the Post Office Department to stay as it is or to become a Crown corporation? Are we going to get out of this never-never land of the Communications Department which is more interested in space vehicles, satellites and new types of communication rather than in the Post Office? Is any member of the government interested in the simple business of writing a letter, putting a stamp on it and mailing it to .someone in the expectation of eventually receiving a
reply to it? Are we to anticipate the establishment of a separate free enterprise organizations which would handle our mail? This possibility is not so remote any longer.
I understand that in the city of Toronto, during the time of the postal strike, hundreds of agencies were set up to deliver mail around the city by car. It was much easier to pay such a company for the service of distributing messages to customers around the city than it was to drop mail in the mailbox. If that was the case when the rate was at six cents a letter, such agencies will find it easier to obtain mail delivery contracts when the Post Office charges eight cents a letter. The entrepreneurs will take an interest in this, and I am sure many arrangements will be made which will have the pony express delivering mail around the major cities rather than the postal employees. All this depends on whether or not the Post Office can operate at eight cents a letter, and it is my guess that unless we bring the employees of the Post Office into the picture they will continue to be confused about the intention of the government with regard to continuing the Post Office as a government department or making it a Crown corporation.
We will have to wait and see how the Post Office department manages on the increased rates that are proposed and how it will manage the labour disputes. They will find that there are many other ways of handling communications within a city as well as from city to city. I we raise the rate to eight cents, we will not penalize a very large sector of the population. You will find that it is the business people who will suffer. Let me give you a small example. An American wrote a letter to a Canadian tourist operator in my area. He wrote that letter fairly early in the year asking for reservations on a certain date. It took 21 days for the operator to receive the letter. He then wrote back confirming the reservation, and that letter took eight days before it got back to the American. The tourist operator sent me the envelope. The destination of the letter was only northern Ohio. I sent this envelope to the Post Office asking them what happened. They are still looking, I presume, because I never had a reply. I am not sure that they can tell what happened because this seems to be a pattern which occurs frequently. Sometimes letters are delivered within a day and a half or two days, but this really shows that the whole system is wrong; it is not reliable. The tourist agent told me that he loses one out of five bookings because he depends totally on the postal service; he cannot use telephone communication. I am sure this is true of a number of other people who depend totally on the postal service.
It seems to me that before we raise our first class mail rates we, as Members of Parliament, should be assured that an over-all plan is being developed which will improve the mail service. When I get a bill from a company, I do not care how long it takes the bill to reach me. If I put a cheque in the envelope and send it back, I do not care if it takes a month for that cheque to reach its destination. This does not worry me, but it may worry the company that is billing me. They may want that
[Mr. Peters.l
June 1, 1971

money now. This must affect many companies because many people have credit cards. It it takes a considerable period of time for the bills to reach the company's customers, the company has much money outstanding.
I suggest that we should look at the problems of our mail service, and assess what we can do about them. We should estimate what it will cost to do something about those problems. We should be in a position to look at some of the ways in which the problems can be solved. We then might find ourselves justified in raising the price of stamps to eight cents on the guarantee that mail is delivered within a reasonable period of time and, if it is not, that it be returned to the Post Office Department which would refund the cost of the stamp. For such a guarantee, I am sure many people would be willing to pay a reasonable postal rate.
If the rate on letters delivered locally is raised from 4 cents to 8 cents next January, all within a period of less than three years, it will entail an abnormally high expenditure for the ordinary public, especially when one considers that they will not get anything like the service that they previously got for 4 cents. In some areas people who live on rural delivery routes have advantages over people living on other routes. If you live on a rural delivery route that does not have too many customers, the likelihood is that you will get mail delivery about three times a week. But if you live on a route which has many more customers you will get mail delivery six times a week. In fact so far as mail delivery is concerned, you may do better living on a rural delivery route than living in a city. I suggest that people living on rural delivery routes should be treated equally. All postal subscribers should get equally good service, no matter where they live.
I hope the minister is able to indicate that the dropping of a large number of small community post offices across Canada has come to an end. I agree that the question of economy was involved. Many of the small post offices were costing much more than they were worth, and it was probably time to examine the services provided by them in relation to the cost. But I suggest that all this had a great adverse effect on many communities. I do not know how many hon. members share my experience, Mr. Speaker, in that the place where I was born no longer exists. It may not have been much of a place to crow about, and my being born there did not add much to it, but it had a sense of community. It existed by virtue of the services provided by the railroad and the post office. These services have now been taken away from it. People still live there but they find it difficult to maintain any type of identity as a community. I am sure my colleagues from western Canada could name hundreds of communities that are in a similar position. The net result may have been a savings for the Postal Department, and in my opinion the amount of savings should have been sufficient to permit normal mail delivery, at the six cent rate for first class mail, to be continued to those communities.
Post Office Act
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Postmaster General will clarify for us the direction in which the department is heading. The country would like to know what is being done. Recently a departmental inspector came into my area, into the town of New Liskeard. It has been designated a bilingual area by the federal government. The inspector came in there, and what did he do? He doesn't look at the hole in the floor of the post office. People have been tripping on that hole. The hole has gone through some kind of plastic coating, and through the plywood beneath that to the original hardwood floor. But the inspector doesn't do anything about that. He says, "We are just renting the building from Public Works; it is the fault of Public Works." Mr. Speaker, it seems it doesn't matter if people fall and break their necks. One lady did fall and was highly embarrassed. When one of the local councillors said she should sue the post office she replied that she was only concerned to get out of the building because of her embarrassment. The inspector says, "You're supposed to have a bilingual notice on the door to show where the postmaster can be found." Mr. Speaker, anybody who ever wanted to see the postmaster had no difficulty finding him. But the inspector insists, and says the French should be at the top of the notice. Maybe that is important, Mr. Speaker. It will be important to that inspector because he will be in lots of trouble. Although it may be a bilingual town the people are not swayed to the extent that they want a major war over Frangais au verso Anglais, or Anglais au verso Frangais. They just want the floor fixed.
I know that the minister is very familiar with the Postal Department. He has a family connection with it. He is sympathetic to the problems of the workers. He has not got his head in the clouds as the former minister in charge of it had. I am sure he has some good suggestions to make. This is a department that must provide service to the public. As long as it remains in the public domain the minister owes us an explanation of his intentions, and of what this large increase in rates will mean to the service provided for the public.

The more common expression is "statutory" holidays. As it now stands, the code provides for eight of these holidays in the year and the proposal in this bill is to add one to the list. speechtext: No St. Jean Baptiste day?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE NINTH GENERAL HOLIDAY WITH PAY
speechtext:
My friend wonders where St. Jean Baptiste day is. Well, it is on June 24 but there is no provision for a holiday in this statute. He is probably recalling the fact that it is on the list of holidays taken by this House of Commons. However, thanks to the helpful interruption of my colleague, I shall point out at this juncture that there is a section in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code under which certain adjustments can be made and some other holiday substituted for one of those set out in the code. It is under the provisions of that section, namely section 28, that in some parts of Canada St. Jean Baptiste day is celebrated rather than one of the holidays listed in the statute.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, that digression is not as much of a digression as it might seem to be because while my bill seeks to extend the list of statutory or general holidays to nine, it keeps alive the provisions of section 28 of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. This means that in any part or region of the country where it was desirable to do so, any holiday more appropriate to a particular area could be substituted for one of the holidays listed. That is all by way of detail.
The purpose of this bill is simple and straightforward. It is a very minimal bill in terms of what it seeks; it asks for just one more general or statutory holiday in the year so that workers who come under federal labour provisions would get nine days in the year instead of eight. The bill specifies that this ninth day would be the first Monday in the month of August. That is a day which is celebrated in many areas of Canada under the title "Civic Holiday" or sometimes it is known as the "August Holiday". It is a little difficult to put a name to it that will meet with general understanding across the country and for that reason in my bill I simply refer to it as the first
Monday in the month of August. That is also the reason for the title of my bill which simply asks to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code in order to provide a ninth holiday with pay.
There is before Parliament at the present time, Mr. Speaker, a bill to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. This bill stands in the name of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). Unfortunately, that bill does not deal with this subject and does not touch on the question of the number of general holidays in a year. I would hope that even if this House is not prepared this afternoon to pass this bill on second reading, that it would see it as appropriate to refer at least the subject matter of the bill to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration in the hope that the committee might add this holiday to the list.
Sir, it is becoming more and more recognized that what we used to regard as adequate in terms of vacations with pay and holidays is no longer the case. There is abundant argument for more time off, for more leisure for our people; there is abundant argument for not only shorter work weeks and more holidays during the working period but for a shorter working life, for early retirement and so on. In the context of the realization that we should be moving in that direction, both to do something about the problem of unemployment and to establish the fact that life is not only for work, my request is a very simple one: it calls for just one more holiday per year. There are already nine holidays specified in the Standing Order of this House for the House of Commons so it seems to me that we should not do any less than that for the workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction.
May I again make the point, and it seems we have to make it every time federal labour law is discussed, that we are not dealing with just the public service. When some newspaper people learn that we have been debating a law regarding workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction they think that means federal public servants. That is not the case. When we speak of federal labour law, we refer to those people who, under the British North America Act, come under federal jurisdiction, such as those who work for the railways, shipping, airlines, in banking and a number of other industries that are clearly set out. Surely, we ought to take the step of providing nine general holidays in the year for these people.
Let it be clear that a part of this package, and this is also set out in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, is that these holidays are to be with pay. There is no point in having holidays without pay. Too many Canadians are experiencing that right now. The provision already in the code with regard to extra pay for people who must work on general holidays would still stand with the amendment that is suggested in this bill.
As I present this bill to the House, Mr. Speaker, it will be pointed out that this is not the first time it has been presented. As a matter of fact, for a good many years now I have been presenting these bills; in the first place o try to get a Canada Labour (Standards) Code and now to amend it. I hope the House is in the mood to say,

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR (STANDARDS) CODE AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE NINTH GENERAL HOLIDAY WITH PAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate this afternoon on Bill C-42, an act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code by the provision of a ninth general holiday with pay.
As the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, I am quite interested and concerned in this general field. It is of more particular interest at the present time because, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, our committee has before it Bill C-228, another bill to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code which was proposed by the government earlier this year. We have commenced hearings on Bill C-228 and in the next few days will be receiving written and oral submissions from a number of main Canadian union and employer associations across the country, including the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, etc.
Government Bill C-228 recommends a number of significant amendments to the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, including the increasing of the minimum wage, initiating 17 weeks maternity leave, strengthened provisions for equal pay for equal work, severance pay and varying lengths of notice with respect to mass lay-offs. However, as the hon. member who just sat down said, Bill C-228 does not make any amendment with respect to the definition of "general holiday" in paragraph F of Section II of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code which now calls for eight general holidays; these are New Year's day, Good Friday, Victoria day, Dominion day, Labour day, Thanksgiving day, Remembrance day and Christmas day and includes any day substituted for any such holiday pursuant to Section 28 of the Code. Bill C-42, which is being debated here this afternoon, would provide for a ninth general holiday under this definition by adding the first Monday in August.
I note that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has introduced similar bills on at least three occasions, according to my information; in April and May, 1967, and September, 1969, but none have been given second reading. When the Canada Labour (Standards) Code first came into effect July 1, 1965, the provision for eight general holidays with pay was far in advance of the number obtained by collective bargaining in federal industries at the time and required a substantial adjustment by the employers under federal jurisdiction.
The proposal for nine holidays is still far in advance of the practice in industry as a whole, although it is apparent that there has been an increase in the number of employees receiving more than eight days holidays since 1965. According to the survey of working conditions conducted by the Canada Department of Labour, only 38 per cent of non-office workers in federal industries received nine holidays or more in 1968. For office workers, the
Canada Labour (Standards) Code figure is 75 per cent. This compares with 17 per cent of non-office workers and 51 per cent of office workers in 1965. In industry as a whole, 56 per cent of non-office workers and 75 per cent of office workers had nine holidays or more in 1968. This compares with 40 per cent for non-office workers and 59 per cent for office workers in 1965.
Only three provinces, Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Alberta, have legislation similar in principle to the federal holiday provisions. Three provinces, Manitoba, Ontario and Nova Scotia, have laid down requirements regarding pay for work done on public holidays. Saskatchewan and British Columbia provide for eight public holidays and Alberta provides for five. Both Manitoba and Ontario require payment of overtime pay for work done on seven public holidays. The Nova Scotia provisions, which are contained in minimum wage orders, require payment of overtime for work on public holidays, but do not stipulate the number of holidays covered. In the United States, the matter of paid general holidays has been left to collective bargaining. The Code provides also that, under certain conditions, an alternative holiday may be substituted for any of the eight holidays specified.
Should a holiday occur on a day on which an employee does not normally work, he must be granted a day off with pay in lieu of the holiday, either at a time convenient to him and his employer or by the addition of a day to his annual vacation. If Christmas, New Year's day or Dominion day falls on a Saturday or Sunday that is a non-working day for an employee, he must be given a holiday with pay on the working day immediately before or after the general holiday. These provisions regarding alternative days off do not apply, however, to employees covered by a collective agreement that entitles them to at least eight paid holidays a year.
The Code lays down the general principle that an employee in a federal undertaking who does not work on a holiday is entitled to his regular pay for the day. If he is paid by the week or month, his wages must not be reduced by reason of his not working on a holiday. If he is paid on any other basis, he must receive the equivalent of a normal day's pay. An employee in a federal undertaking who is required to work on a general holiday, other than one employed in a "continuous operation", is entitled to his regular wages for the day and, in addition, to time and one-half his regular rate for all time worked. In effect, he is paid two and one-half times his usual rate.
An employee employed in a "continuous operation", defined to include employment concerned with the operation of trains, planes, ships, trucks and other vehicles, telephone, radio, television, and telegraph services, or any other service normally carried on without regard to Sundays or holidays, who is required to work on a holiday either must be paid his regular wages for the day, plus time and one-half his regular rate for all time worked or, in addition to his regular pay for the day, must be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which can be either a day added to his annual vacation or another day convenient to him and his employer.

June 1, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
There are some situations in which an employee is not entitled to holiday pay. An employee is not entitled to pay for a general holiday that occurs in his first 30 days of employment with an employer, but if he is required to work on a holiday he must be paid time and one-half his regular rate. If he is employed in a continuous operation, he may be paid at his regular rate for work done on a holiday. A further exception is that an employee is not entitled to pay for a general holiday on which he does not work if he is not entitled to wages for at least 15 days during the 30 calendar days immediately preceding the holiday. An employee in a continuous operation is not entitled to pay for a general holiday if he did not report for work in response to a call from the employer.
Special regulations for longshoremen provide that a longshoreman employed by an employer who is not a member of a "Multi-employer unit" is entitled to holiday pay if he is entitled to wages for at least 15 days or 120 hours in the 30 calendar days immediately preceding a general holiday. Pay for the holiday may not be less than eight times the employee's basic hourly wage rate. A longshoreman employed by an employer who is not a member of a "multi-employer unit" must be paid, on each payday, in lieu of general holidays, an amount equal to 3 per cent of his basic wage rate multiplied by the number of hours he has worked for the employer in the pay period. An employee who is required to work on a general holiday is to be paid at not less than one and one-half t mes his basic rate of wages for the time worked by him on that day.
From the figures I quoted earlier of 38 per cent of non-office workers in federal industries and 75 per cent of office workers in federal industries receiving nine holidays or more in 1968 and, in industry as a whole, with 56 per cent of non-office workers and 75 per cent of office workers receiving nine holidays or more, I would think that the time is fast approaching for the federal government to further amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code to add at least one more, a ninth holiday. I believe, also, that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should be congratulated for keeping this matter before the House of Commons in recent years. While he can often be criticized for private bills which propose considerable additional benefits, either in money or otherwise, out of all relationship to the practical realities of the day, I believe that in this case he is coming pretty close to a realistic mark in advocating the amendment of the Code to include a ninth general holiday for industries under federal jurisdiction.
I know that in Ontario, and I believe in many other parts of the country, a large proportion of employees, including most office employees, have obtained the first Monday of August as a holiday, known as Civic Holiday, for a number of years. The first Monday in August is particularly welcome as a holiday because it gives another long summer weekend in between the Dominion day, July 1 holiday, and the Labour day holiday on the first Monday of September. The workers, particularly in our large urban areas in southern Canada, look forward to a long holiday weekend about the first of August to get away from the often very oppressive heat in the cities to
the lakes and resorts districts. Accordingly, since in 1968 by the aforementioned figures considerably more than half the employees in general had this first Monday in August as a holiday, I would certainly think that it is about time that we amended the Canada Labour (Standards) Code to include this as a ninth general holiday as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read with interest the bill presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He indicated that I am back at the old stand. I think he made that somewhat derogatory remark because I participate in the debates in private members' hour. I can assure him that this is a compliment to him. I have heard him say on more than one occasion that this is a good opportunity to participate in the cut and thrust of a debate. The hon. member is well known for his talent and ability in the debating field. One appreciates the opportunity to match wits, talent and ability with a man of such long experience in this chamber.
The hon. member indicated that, in effect, this amendment applies to those who come under federal jurisdiction. He then went on to point out that this is not limited to federal civil servants. When this kind of suggestion is put forward, it has the effect of acting as a guideline for other jurisdictions. I sometimes wonder whether creating this kind of false holiday makes the small businessman wince a bit. It is my guess that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has never been a small businessman and, therefore, has not been faced with the difficulties of meeting these particular paid holidays. The hon. member would be right to correct me and say that this particular piece of legislation does not apply to small businessmen, but I suggest it is the thin edge of the wedge that would be used by workers employed by small businessmen to bring about the number of holidays that he is recommending.
If I might digress for a moment, the hon. member referred to the fact that we in this chamber have nine or 10 holidays. Frankly, that is not a fair comparison. Many of the holidays provided find the members back in the ridings participating as Members of Parliament in one function or another. In many cases, they can hardly be called holidays. I think that most members of this chamber within appropriate travelling distance are able to go back to their ridings and participate in Remembrance Day services. Although it is a holiday from the House, it is not a holiday as far as the members are concerned. They participate in the services, albeit this is something they like to do. However, it can hardly be described as a holiday.
I believe in having as much leisure time as possible. However, as I have indicated on more than one occasion, I was raised in a mining community where fathers and

June 1, 1971

older brothers worked a seven day week. We accepted this because it was automatic for dad to go to work every day. We were happy that he was able to be home on Christmas day. In many instances, particularly in the mining communities in northern Ontario, Christmas was the one and only day that was recognized as a holiday. There comes a time when we have to look at what I call false holidays, when we are creating holidays for the sake of leisure time. We must not go too far and create a detrimental effect by lowering productivity, thus making it possible for the employed to become unemployed because the small businessmen cannot cope with all these holidays. We must bear in mind that the small businessmen would have to hire others to fill the gaps on more than one occasion.
I take exception to the timing of this particular holiday, if the bill is carried. It has been suggested that the holiday be on the first Monday in August. The hon. member who spoke before me and the mover of this bill have indicated that the first Monday of August would be the appropriate time. I do not believe this proposal takes into consideration what we in Canada all know, namely the severe winters. If we are going to have another holiday rather than Victoria day. It is time we started the mood of vacation and holiday. Even though an individual has to work in July and August, there is a certain relaxed atmosphere, something that is not evident in the months of February and March, toward the end of a long winter. If the holiday proposed in this bill is adopted, I will move an amendment that some consideration be given having it sometime in February.
There is another aspect of holidays which disturbs me. This particular holiday has not been given a name. I notice that July 1 has not been given a name. The May 24 holiday is sometimes referred to as the 24th of May holiday rather than Victoria day. It is time we started looking at these general holidays with a view to giving them names and honouring different ideas and themes. I would like to see the name of Victoria day changed. It could be given a name that would pay respect to the men who won the liberty that we all enjoy and appreciate so much today, namely the veterans of this country. I do not think that members of the army, navy or air force would object if this were called the Battle of Vimy Ridge day or Dieppe day. I would like to see these men recognized so that each year the young people would ask why we have a Vimy Ridge or Dieppe day. We could stress the contribution that was made by our Canadian fighting men during those days. It would have much more significance and would operate as a unifying force, much more so than using a name such as Victoria day.
There is a great deal of debate at the present time about July 1. It is called many things. Here it is called Dominion day. This would be a glorious opportunity to honour the men who gave us the freedom and opportunity to work so that we can appreciate the eight, nine, 10 or more holidays which we get annually. To avoid any interservice jealousy, I would suggest a name such as veterans day.
Remembrance day has special significance. It is my hope that we will never change the idea of the eleventh
Canada Labour (Standards) Code hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month. That has a particular significance. It is not the kind of day where we should try to accommodate the working man in order that he will have a long weekend. I hope Remembrance day will always be on the same day as at present. In this way, when people ask why we have a holiday in the middle of the week and have two minutes silence at eleven o'clock on November 11, we will continue to be able to give an answer to the young people who have not known a time of war and hopefully never will.
It is not often that I agree with a gentleman we see over television from time to time, namely Gordon Sinclair. I hope that one day we will have a holiday that will be called flag day. I am not so naive as to think that after the bitter debate that surrounded the flag, the partisan politics brought to play and the viciousness of the attack and counterattack that this is apt to happen overnight. There are probably still many memories in this House of that particular debate. There are still some feelings against the flag. However, the day will come when we will all be proud of the flag. When that time comes, I hope we will have a flag day.
I was pleased to see the Kinsmen Club of Stoney Creek have a project to sponsor the idea of a flag day. They, as did Gordon Sinclair, suggested that it take place sometime in February, primarily because it would give a holiday to the workingman at that time of the year when the workingman is really looking for a holiday. It would have the effect of honouring the flag we have come to know as the flag of Canada, distinctly, uniquely and proudly Canadian. The hon. member who moved this bill has indicated that there is really not much scope for debate. In fact, it seems to boil down to the question whether we are going to pass this bill and thus create this particular holiday or we are not.
I am going to vote against the bill at this stage because I think other things should be done first. I sincerely believe that thought has to be given to chang ng the names of some of our holidays, as we understand them, so as to give them meaning in the way I have suggested, namely, to pay tribute to the veterans to whom we owe so much and whom all too often we have a tendency to forget. You cannot blame the young people for this, Mr. Speaker. With them it is not a question of forgetting but, rather, of never knowing about the contribution made by our veterans. Although I was not living at the time of the First World War, as a result of my experience during the Second World War, in which I lost friends and knew others who participated in the armed forces, I obtained a new insight into, a new interest in and, more important than anything, a new appreciation of our veterans.
It is unfortunate that we had to have a Second World War so that someone like myself could have a second look at our veterans and recognize the contribution made by what we have called our "old sweats", the veterans of the First World War. If we put into these holidays the kind of respect that I think our veterans deserve, then perhaps it will be better than giving the workingman an

June 1, 1971
Canada Labour (Standards) Code
extra day's holiday. Perhaps on more than one occasion during the year we shall say to our veterans that we are paying tribute not only to those who gave their lives but also to those who gave their time and effort, even parts of their bodies, in order to protect this country. We would tell them that we have not forgotten. And to those people who never knew them or had the opportunity to forget, we are pointing out the contribution they made. One small way in which we could do this is by changing the name of some of our holidays.
The hon. member who spoke before me must have had the same research material as I, because some of the comments that I wanted to make he covered in his usual comprehensive way, obviously the result of a tremendous amount of work done this afternoon or last night. I pay tribute to him for the fine job he is doing as chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. Needless to say, I will not insult his presentation by reiterating the points that he made. I have tried to make my point; I hope I have done so effectively and I thank the House for its attention.

Why not set up normal wage rates for those heads of families who, because they work, are denied all kinds of supplementary benefits they could get if they were unemployed or depended on welfare allowances.
I would much rather encourage someone who is willing to work, who takes the trouble and has the courage to earn his family's living. I would rather help him than the chronically unemployed. I am not talking about those who are sick and are entitled to welfare allowances; there are exceptions. However, some people never want to work.
I had evidence of that a few times this winter. I hired a man for a three-to four-hour job. He was a man of good build, the same as mine, he was 28 years old, he had two
Canada Labour (Standards) Code children and he was on welfare. I asked him casually: Do you want to work? He said he did. And so, I referred his case to the manager of the Manpower Centre in Montreal. Now, can you imagine what the answer of the manager was after 12 days? "We made four appointments with him and he did not show up for a single one." I had to tell the manager to forget about it. This is another chronic case, another parasite of society. I know what social welfare is all about. I come from a workmen's district, a district with citizens' committees and dissenters. I support these increased benefits in the case of people who are really in need. A 62-year-old widow recently came to my office. Since there is no legislation applicable to her case, I refered her to the local welfare office. She started crying and she told me: "Listen, Mr. Loiselle, while my husband was alive, we never had much money, that's true, but we never had to go on welfare. Well, he is dead, and here I am". Mr. Speaker, this is a very well-intentioned bill, I am sure, but for the life of me I cannot understand how one can pick a day out of thin air and call it a national day of a day of special significance which merits being made a holiday. It makes me wonder about the purpose behind suggestions which encourage us to manufacture a holiday in order to get another day off.
To my mind, the words "the first Monday in the month of August" represent a nameless, pointless, meaningless and purposeless day. I cannot see how we could support a bill, even one to name an additional day under the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, such as this. If we want another day off for federal government employees, then let us give them a day off under the general provisions of the federal code. Surely it is not necessary to go through this terrible travesty.
I say this with all respect to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) because, as I said earlier, I am sure his intention is good. What we would be doing here would be adding another day to the general holidays of New Year's day, Good Friday, Labour day, Thanksgiving day, Remembrance day and Christmas day which for hundreds of years have become meaningful to people. We would be saying that there is another great day in Canada, which is the first Monday in the month of August.
I do not see how I could support this bill. I wonder whether the bill would qualify if we accepted it as one of Robert L. Ripley's Believe-it-or-Nots by saying we have the longest name for a holiday in the world, called "The first Monday in the month of August."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to support the bill that is before us. I agree in principle that the postal services should be efficient and modern. Indeed, I agree with the principle that the user should pay and I hope that the Post Office can achieve that objective.
I am rising to ask the minister some questions which I hope he will answer either in summing up the debate or when the bill is before the committee. I should like to begin by quot ng what the minister said yesterday when speaking in this debate:
The Post Office is relying heavily on marketing principles to determine the needs of customers and to tailor services to meet these needs.
I wish to tell the minister about a need which is not being met by the Post Office and about a service which is needed. It is one within my own constituency, in the

June 1, 1971
Post Office Act
community of Thorneliffe Park which now contains
14,000	people. If they lived alone and not in the heart of Toronto, the lack of attention which is being given to their needs might be considered scandalous. I suggest that the problem is all the more serious because they are located in the heart of an important city.
These 14,000 people have no postal services whatsoever. I should like to tell hon. members something about their history. Until about a year ago they were served by a postal substation. Then the substation was closed because it was too crowded, in view of the demand, to provide the kind of service that was required. It was not able to do the job-everyone agreed that this was so- particularly at Christmas, but all year round it was too busy and too crowded to do its job properly. Therefore it was closed.
It was replaced by two stamp machines. At first there was one stamp machine. It was inadequate because it would run out of stamps every few hours, that is to say, it required servicing more than once a day. So a second stamp machine was added. These 14,000 individuals, for whom marketing principles are being studied to determine the needs of customers and to tailor services to meet their needs, now have two machines which contain enough stamps for nearly one whole day.
In the speech to which I have already referred, the minister said:
We have long-range plans to replace Inadequate mail. .. facilities in major cities with up to date plants.
I hope there is a short-range plan to replace these two stamp machines with an adequate facility to cover the needs of 14,000 people. There is a range of innovative services about which the minister told us.
He referred to the Fairview mall boutique, a postal boutique which will provide government departments and agencies with an opportunity to disseminate information. I submit it is most unfair that the Fairview mall, which is not greater than Thorneliffe Park, should have a postal boutique which provides a wide range of services when the 14,000 people of Thorneliffe Park have only two stamp machines which run out of stamps before the end of the day.
Recently the minister indicated that work was being done to try and provide better facilities for Thorneliffe Park. In fact, for over a year there has been a search for a new location for the post office. But a year is too long. Physically, this is a small community. The number of alternative locations is quite limited and it should not take a year for a decision to be made, for negotiations to be concluded and for a post office to be provided.
A few months ago I tabled the following question in the House of Commons:
Has the government established any deadline tor obtaining a post office facility for Thorneliffe Park?
After the question had lain on the order paper for several months, the answer I received was a very simple one. It was "no"-one word.
In his address yesterday the minister indicated that a program to improve the services and appearance of small post offices is scheduled to get under way in July. Here we are, looking to July to improve the appearance and services of existing small post offices. I would like to close on this note and remind the minister that the 14,000 people of Thorneliffe Park are not waiting for an extra stamp machine, they are not waiting for a boutique or for services and facilities based on marketing principles: they are simply waiting for a post office and I submit they should have one.
