subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STAMP AGENTS' COMMISSION, LETTER MAIL PREPARATION ARRANGEMENTS, EXTRAORDINARY SERVICES, MEMBERS' MAIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to speak on the legislation now before us.
The minister is seeking passage of a bill providing that postal rates for first class mail be increased from 6 to 7 cents, effective July 1, 1971, and from 7 to 8 cents, effective January 1, 1972. This increase is about the only concern, or at least the main one, of this government, which sponsors the legislation now before us. It is not very much concerned, however, about services to be provided to mail users.
What the people require of the Post Office is fast and efficient service. It seems that since 1954 especially, postal rates have increased periodically and as they go up, the
service gets worse.
I do not know exactly what is wrong, if influences outside the postal administration interfere with its operation, but the fact is that the postal service is not efficient right now.
In fact, I have heard from time to time in the House some members convey to the minister complaints made by their electors to the effect that the mail is moving slower and slower. The minister then replied: If you bring specific cases to my attention, I shall investigate and we shall attempt to correct the situation.
Now, I have in my hand an article which I sent to one of my constituents. I admit that it was no first class correspondence but, nevertheless, according to the House of Commons post-mark the item was mailed May 6 at 4 P.M. and reached Authier on May 18, 1971. I think this is much too long to dispatch an item from Ottawa to a community in Abitibi. What is the reason for such a state of affairs? I think that once I have expressed this complaint to the hon. minister in a moment, if his officials want to take the trouble to do so they will find the cause of this delay.
This is not the only case. I believe that if an inquiry is made at the level of city regional offices, we shall find there the main reason for the inefficiency of the postal service. It is not up to me to criticize the employees of these big offices, but it is obvious that if postal workers in small towns or villages worked in the same spirit as those in the large post offices, we simply would not have any postal service.
I think there is much room for improvement in this field. Why are those workers not more efficient? Is it on account of low morale, or because their training officer did not do a good job?

June 1, 1971

We could compare this to a recent incident that occurred within the Canadien hockey team. At one time, there were complaints that if the team was not as efficient as it should be, it was due to the coach who did not have the knack to get the best out of his players.
I wonder whether it is not the same with postal workers and whether, at a given time, there was not a lack of leadership to boost and support their morale.
e (8:20 p.m.)
At all events, the fact remains that services have been considerably downgraded in spite of constantly increasing rates, labour and machinery costs and raw material requirements. We are therefore justified in asking what is wrong and what can be done.
A few years ago, the former Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) called on K. P. Warwick and Company to conduct studies on ways and means of improving the postal service. The company carried out 15 studies within the 12 months ending on November 1, 1969, at which date it submitted a report. It called on the services of six consultant firms in order to seek solutions to be applied to the problem. Apparently, however, the conclusion was that the Post Office Department should be transformed into a Crown corporation in order to provide efficient service on a self-sustaining basis. Indeed, the minister mentioned in the statement he made upon introducing this bill that if the postal rates were not increased this year, the deficit would add up to some $113 million for
1971-72. Aslo it is said in the report on the study that if changes are not made before 1975, the deficit could well reach $500 million.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know to what extent the cabinet has considered the report submitted by this firm nor what conclusions were arrived at, but, in any event, this report would deserve careful examination to determine whether it would be wise to make the corrections that are mentioned, since those experts which have studied the question certainly did not make their suggestions merely to have them ignored. The suggestions should be considered very carefully to see whether it would be desirable to make such changes, in order not to ensure a profit but to avoid a deficit.
According to the estimates in this report, it could happen that we shall have to pay 12 cents for a stamp in 1980 and 21 cents in 1990 in order to keep revenues at a sensible level corresponding to increasing costs.
According to the experts who have studied the matter thoroughly, it seems that this service will be more and more expensive yet without any guarantee of efficiency.
In his opening remarks the minister told us that it was necessary to increase rates for users of postal services so that those who do not use them do not have to subsidize them. The minister said that industries, tradespeople and businessmen accounted for 80 p. 100 of the volume of mail and the rest of the population for the other 20 p. 100.
I understand both the position and the purpose of the minister. However, he knows very well that if postal rates are increased for industries, tradespeople and busi-
Post Office Act
nessmen, the increase will be reflected in their cost prices and the consumer will be once more paying for it. The consumer always pays in the end for any increment. Whether he does so through public funds or higher consumer prices, the effect is nearly the same.
The increase of postal rates will only bring temporary relief and will not really solve the problem, because I expect that the administration costs of the postal system will continue to increase as those of any other system and even if the department were turned into a Crown corporation, it would be confronted with the same increases or the same requests for increases.
In my opinion, the government should try to find some practical and effective procedures to dispatch as quickly as possible the mail from a point to another, in order that the people who need those services to communicate with each another will quickly obtain them, otherwise they will resort to other means of communication. The rates will then be increased and the users will be tempted to use other means of communication.
I do not think the bill now before us brings the changes the public is expecting. It will do nothing more than ease the financial situation of that department trying to finance itself. We should not be more demanding of such a service as far as profitability is concerned than of any other department. The Department of External Affairs, the Secretary of State or the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are not required to pay their own way, so why should we ask the Post Office Department to have no deficit?
Even if public funds must make up a few deficits, the people will not care too much about it, but we must first of all try to give them the satisfactory services they want.

subtopic: POST OFFICE ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING STAMP AGENTS' COMMISSION, LETTER MAIL PREPARATION ARRANGEMENTS, EXTRAORDINARY SERVICES, MEMBERS' MAIL, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin my remarks in French since we are discussing a department which is now under a Frenchspeaking minister and I think you can get along better with him in French than in English, although I notice he is wearing his earphone.
The bill now before us aims at raising postal rates. We are being told that the minister wants to do something which should have been done long ago. He has delayed raising the commission to be paid to agents selling postage stamps in small sub-offices. As much as 5 per cent will be paid in commission for some stamp sales.
Those people will take advantage of the opportunity and doubtless many people will want to sell stamps. Often one has trouble obtaining stamps, especially when they are sold through machines offering 24 cents' worth of stamps for 25 cents. Now, what is the minister going to sell the public since the cost of stamps will be increased to 7 cents? Will we get only three 7-cent stamps and three 1-cent stamps? What stamps will the booklets contain?

However, Mr. Speaker, various items are provided for in this bill. I have no great cause for complaint in my relations with the Post Office Department. I must say, though, that I join with hon. members who feel that for

June 1, 1971
Post Office Act
the last two or three years, particularly under the minister's predecessor, there has been a myth to the effect that the Post Office Department should show a profit regardless of the level of service.
The postal service, Mr. Speaker, was never founded to provide a profit. We have seen the paradox of rapidly escalating letter and parcel postage rates and charges for special services, and a decline in the quality of general services. Almost all members have complained about the time lapse between picking up and delivering mail. One does not rely any more on such things as overnight service. That service used to be provided as a natural course of events, but it is not any more. There was a local rate for overnight service, but now there is no local rate: instead there is poorer service.
I would refer to the time of the passport muddle. Never did one section of the government service join more in what I frankly fear were the inefficiencies of another department than did the postal service, particularly with regard to registrations. At that time, once a passport had left Ottawa in a bulk billing under registration it could end up in Timbuctu and nobody would be any the wiser. This happened in many instances. Passports went astray and were never found simply because there was no way of backtracking under the bulk billing.
I was promised that there would be some sort of improvement in the services in order that items could be followed up, but it would be at an increased rate and not at the registered rate. Services that had been standard before, or had been standard in certain communities where bulk billings did not apply, were to be upgraded, but we were also to upgrade the charges.
That was pure and absolute nonsense, Mr. Speaker, and was not justified under any circumstance. We know that items started out in small communities as registered items, then came to a main postal station, a distributing point and disappeared. If a letter were sent, say from a small town in Alberta to eastern Canada, it would reach Edmonton then join a bulk billing and disappear. It would be gone. Unless they searched the postal stations from the roof to the basement, the item could be gone forever: it was just lost. Yet we were being charged the same rate by the post office.
I have not heard of any new, improved service although it is possible there is one. The passport division has improved its efficiency and therefore we are not bound to search for passports as we were wont to do on previous occasions when it was always wise to send out the registration number because that, at least, was half a clue.
Then one runs up against certain regulations in the postal service. Some think, Mr. Speaker, that these regulations were written on the same tablets as those on which Moses put down the commandments of God, so sacred are they. They are treated with the greatest of reverence by postal officials. When you talk to postal

officials about these regulations you learn that they assume that Parliament has considered and approved them. Of course, we know that is totally false.
The regulations are made at home for home use and for the benefit of home, that is, for the benefit of those administering the regulations. That is surprising. I have talked with some of the senior people in the department-I do not mean here in Ottawa but across the country-and laid it on the line that the Post Office provides a service for the public and that the word that must be underscored three or four times is "service". The public does not exist for the benefit of the Post Office, although a great number of Post Office personnel operate on that basis. Many of them feel that the great, unwashed public is there for their personal benefit and gratification, on the basis of the regulations.
It is not pleasant to say these things, and I know that many of the minister's officials are listening. I would tell them the same thing face to face. I have said it many times over the telephone. The one cardinal rule that you must apply, not only in the post office but in other departments of government is the rule of service to the public. The regulations should be designed to provide service; they should not be made to inhibit service. There must be that degree of flexibility which will permit service to be extended. Let there be none of this business: You happen to be 50 feet beyond a certain boundary line and therefore we cannot deliver mail to your door. That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the self-serving regulations made for the benefit of those at home within the department.
I know that within its administration the department must also deal with groups of employees who come under collective bargaining but who have forgotten the word "service". As a matter of fact, the leader of one of these groups the other night said he could not care less about service or about the efficiency of the department; his interest lay merely in getting more money for his men. That type of demagogy just will not do. This is a service department. It is organized not for the benefit of administrators and employees but for the benefit of the public. And who are the public but the people of Canada? This is a service for the people of this country.
If everyone within the department adopted the same attitude toward service that has been exhibited by some of the men whom we have seen performing in the last couple of years, this would indeed become a sad, sad country. Unfortunately, there is an attitude of: Forget the women and children. Cast off the lifeboat because I'm in it. I could use much more, shall we say, crude expressions to illustrate the same attitude. That attitude is not right. It will not do to say: I'm all right; cast off. Forget about the others.
One point I would make to the minister is that right from the top of the organization under his jurisdiction there should be a re-examination of the motivation behind the regulations. These should be designed to give service with maximum efficiency and more than just a modicum af courtesy.
June 1, 1971

What are the public concerned about? They are concerned about the little things-rudeness and curtness and the fact that they cannot pick up their mail. A Member of Parliament provides the crying-towel for many of these complaints. These people are not going to make the complaints to their local postmaster, regardless of the size of town. They do not know the postmaster; he is a man in a back office. Timid little ladies or young persons who are not used to facing up to situations are not going to complain. Usually a strip is torn off them or someone indicates that they are soreheads. They usually come to their Member of Parliament to complain.
It is great to listen to these things but it is a sad reflection on what should be one of the jewels in the crown of services which the government provides. That is where the postal service should be. Of all the services the government can provide with almost daily repetition, the postal service should be uppermost; but unfortunately this is not the case.
For the second time in four years the public of Canada is faced with an increase in postage rates. This increase will be made pretty well across the board; it will affect the majority of the public. There were famous, or infamous incidents in 1967 or 1968. There is a rather sad history of a certain night here. I am sure the minister will always remember that. But there has not been an improvement in service. The only plea I make is insistence upon service. I will repeat it as often as is necessary. We cannot expect the public to come to us just because the postal services are there. If you have a service, you have to sell it by your attitude, courtesy and efficiency. In this way you have a much more successful and happier operation.
Some of the measures adopted have been gifts laid at the foot of the altar of efficiency. They have been appalling because they have not succeeded. There may appear to be some efficiency. But ask John Q. Public what he thinks! Although he pays more, he does not get his mail any quicker. I realize that salaries, and so forth, have escalated. One wonders when the demands are going to stop. However, equipment and productivity have increased. There may have been a case for an increase at some time, but at the moment the minister has not demonstrated an absolute need. It is incumbent upon the government to prove their case for an increase in postal rates.
There are clarifications of the law with regard to postal services that will be available to members of this House. There are some idiosyncracies in this respect. There is one provision of which I fully approve because I have seen abuses in the past. The franking privileges of members will cease ten days after dissolution of Parliament. In the past almost whole political campaigns have been launched from Ottawa. This was handy for members who had a geographical advantage. That is not fair. I think this provision will be much better for everybody. I fully approve of the limitation to be imposed on this service for Members of Parliament.

It is up to the minister to make his case with regard to the increase in rates, not merely quoting grandiose figures. I want to see something demonstrable in the case of improved services. Will there be an improvement? To use a current phrase, I am still very much "out to lunch" with regard to the numbering code in Ottawa. Frankly, I receive very little mail from Ottawa which includes this code. The reason is that it is too complicated. It may be very simple for those who are in contact with the plan, but I have to stop and think very hard whether I have the letters and digits in their proper sequence. I even have to ask myself what they are; there are many combinations.
We must remember that these codes are not printed; they are written. One which I recall is K1H 5S8. When they are handwritten, the "5," "S" and "8" look very much the same. I think a sorter would have to make a triple examination of the 5S8 because of their similarity. These are some of the practical difficulties. Most of my neighbours put the notice which they received into a drawer. They found it too complicated to bother with it. They were quite happy with the postal zone they used before.
There many be some theoretical advantages in this system but unless the public is persuaded that it will be used generally and is to their advantage, it is of no use. I admit that perhaps more testing is required. It might be necessary to send out a few more reminders to the public. Very nice kits with little stickers were distributed. There are two cabinet ministers who live on my street. I wonder how many of those stickers are still in desk drawers in their homes. I cannot persuade my wife to use them. She says that she cannot remember the code. The same applies to my neighbours. Theoretically, this plan may be perfectly good but greater effort has to be made to sell it. At the moment, I must confess it is a bit of a non-starter. It may be all right in government offices.
When letters go out from our offices on Parliament Hill to our constituents, we use the new postal code. My correspondents have asked me what these symbols mean because they have not heard about them. I know they have been publicized in the press here and perhaps mention has been made of them in the press generally, but how many people remember that sort of thing? I would have to write a special letter to each of my correspondents in Edmonton and ask them please to use the code number, and I just cannot do it. Again let me say I do not think the minister has demonstrated the need for these increases in postal rates. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I think much of it is due to mismanagement. I think this House and the country is faced with deciding whether the Post Office Department is to be run as a service to the Canadian people or made to pay like a business organization. I have no doubt at all that the Post Office must be run as a service to the Canadian public and that we should expect to have deficits. If we are to supply service to outlying areas and to rural parts of Canada, in many instances it is simply impossible to make the service a paying proposition. I would be the first to admit that rural areas deserve small post offices and postal services because, after all, these people have pioneered this country and are entitled to some of the amenities of life. If we have to operate such services at a loss, as we do in many cases, I submit there is absolutely nothing wrong with doing so.
When the minister closes this debate I would also ask him to outline to the House exactly what are his plans, not just for next year but for the next few years. Where are we going, and where are the rates going to stop? Is the minister trying to put this department on a paying basis in order that it will show figures in the black every year? If this is the desire of the department it should let members of the House and the people of the country know what to expect. So far we have not been given the complete picture by the new Postmaster General or his predecessor.
Le me refer again briefly to the point I raised last night. The post office box rental charge to residents of rural areas is unjust. Let me make it crystal clear that as a result of studying postal revenue sources for 1970 in Canada as reported in the annual report of the Post Office, I found that $4.9 million were collected from post office box rentals, mainly from people living in rural areas. Again I suggest to the minister that when people living in rural areas are charged this amount for the rental of post office boxes they are being discriminated against by the government.
I have my mail delivered to my apartment in Ottawa. It is slipped through the door and I pick it up in the morning. People in rural areas should be assured that the mail delivered to small post offices can be picked up if necessary some time after the post office is closed, and without cost. They should be in a position to receive mail on a general delivery basis. They should have exactly the same service which people in the cities receive. Our Post Office is not giving these people this service.
I make this point as strongly as I can and suggest it is rank discrimination against the people living in rural areas. The department is suggesting to them that they must accept this kind of service charge because they have chosen to live in rural areas rather than in larger
June 1, 1971

centres. There is no rhyme or reason in the philosophy of the Post Office Department which maintains this discriminatory practice. Let me again remind the minister that this charge amounted to only 1.1 per cent of the total revenue of the department in the fiscal year 196970. By changing the system, the department might increase its deficit by a small amount but this should be absorbed by the system if the department intends to deal fairly with people who live in villages and rural areas.
I do not intend to continue my remarks because we will have an opportunity to talk about this situat on after the bill has been sent to committee and reported back to the House. I trust that when the minister closes the debate he will tell us where the Post Office Department is going and how it will get there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on Bill C-240 as regards the hike in postal rates and certain services which are likely to be provided to hon. members should this measure be adopted.
I find it highly regrettable that the minister in charge of the Post Office-for whom I have the greatest respect-is the sponsor of a bill whose chief purpose is increasing postal rates.
However, no matter how imaginative one may be, one cannot find any improvement in postal services which would warrant this boost. I am referring more specifically to the services which should be improved and which have not been since the last raise.
Honorable members will recall that when the former Postmaster General introduced a bill to increase postal rates, we warned the government that such a measure would bring about an increase in the dailies' subscription rates. The government replied that there would not be any direct effects on subscription rates to daily newspapers. And yet, it is exactly what happened in the rural areas and as we had been telling the government all along, in the long run, the small taxpayer had to pay for it.
However, everyone knows now that it is precisely what happened and the daily papers, at least those in my area, now cost twice what they used to cost and the newspaper owners are saying that the increase is due to the high cost of delivery by mail.
It will also be remembered that, at that time, the president of Le Soleil of Quebec City was sending us, every day, three feet long telegrams. I even measured one, and it was 38 inches long, in which he asked us to oppose that measure.
At that time, it was the hon. members who had benefited the most from free publicity in that newspaper during the 1968 election campaign who were supporting the bill. As a matter of fact, they were supporting it because of the party line, as, deep down, they were not in favour of the bill. On the other hand, those who were against it, the hon. member for Bellechasse among others, were those who got the least out of that free publicity. Those hon. members opposed the measure not because they had
Post Office Act
obligations or through gratitude to the press, but because they knew beforehand that it would be the "small people" who would pay for the increase.
There is another thing we deplore, but unfortunately it is too late to do anything about it. If today we could be assured that the Canadian people would get a better service, we would certainly be confident and probably would support the increase because we would be convinced that in so doing we would give to the government and the Post Office an apportunity to offer a better service to the people, thus giving them a satisfaction they deserve.
We have now reached the point where we think twice before sending out bulk mail and figure on a 10 day delay to make sure it will be delivered on time. And we find that even if we allow for the necessary delays, delivery is still late.
I found out once that 50 per cent of the notices for a meeting were delivered two days after the meeting was held. I then asked the Postmaster General, following complaints from my constituents, if there was any possibility of making an inquiry to determine why those notices were not delivered on time. The Postmaster General, through his officials, authorized the investigation and they reported to me.
I must say I was happy with the way the investigation was carried out and also with the officials' performance of their duties, since they reported to me. I was just waiting for an opportunity to remind the Postmaster General-or rather his predecessor, that we express criticisms and suggestions only after having thoroughly gone into the matter-to use the words of a great one who has passed away-in order to cause prejudice to no one and not to make unjustified criticisms.
In such circumstances, when deliveries are not on time, the sender is dissatisfied, and so are those who are to receive the communications, both sender and addressee are discontented.
As representatives of the people we must, on occasion, report on the situation and try to call for improvements. The way things are, no wonder the public loses confidence in the postal service. The Minister is right being concerned about it. He is frank enough to say it publicly as he did yesterday in this House, as may be seen from page 6216 of Hansard, and I quote:
. .. one which concerns me greatly is the loss of public confidence the Post Office has experienced in recent years. As I have said before, this confidence must be restored if the Post Office is to be able to continue its vital role in Canadian society. To this end, we are moving to improve services through major reforms.
I am convinced that the minister is well meaning, that he wants to make major reforms, but these should not merely consist in raising postage rates. It would be necessary, indeed, to improve the postal service so that it might regain public confidence and be more widely used because, on the whole, when I was younger, I considered

June 1, 1971
Post Office Act
this service as a sacred one. When we mailed something, it could reach its destination without any concern. If any item got lost, it was possible to find it without too much difficulty by filing our complaints to the postmaster or the authorities.
The minister also said, and I quote:
Government has to decide if the taxpayers of this country should subsidize services whose main users are business and industry. Approximately 80 per cent of Post Office volumes are in fact derived from business and industry. Given this, the principle of successive operating deficits, to be supported by general taxation, would appear inequitable.
Mr. Speaker, even if the main users belong to the business and industrial sectors, the fact remains that under this procedure, in the field of business and industry, costs increase to the same extent and the consumer ends up footing the bill. If I were in business, if my operating costs increased because of higher postal rates, as a businessman, I would have to put in the expenditures column, higher expenses, so that these could be added in the end to my income. This would also apply to the manufacturing cost if I were in the industrial field. I would indirectly ask the consumer to cover them, which is normal.
Although it is said that 80 per cent of the mail is sent out by business people and industries, it is however the population that indirectly pays for it. If I were convinced that the increase mentioned in the bill would provide towns of about 1,000 people with the services of a post office, I would perhaps be more favourable to this legislation.
I would like here to appeal to the minister and make several requests that I have expressed before and which he has understood very well. However, he is unable to answer members' requests concerning the building of new post offices. If I were quite sure that those increases would finally be used to enable the minister to meet those rightful demands, I would have, in all fairness, to trust him and give him the support he needs under the circumstances.
In addition, the minister referred-and rightly-to the purchasing power of the dollar to justify that increase and I quote:
In terms of the purchasing power of the dollar, the basic increase of seven and eight cents is actually lower than the four cent rate which came into effect in 1954.
I am quite pleased to read what the minister said in that connection, Mr. Speaker. He takes into account the increased cost of living, the depreciation of the dollar to justify increased demand as far as the postal service is concerned. However, the same factor should also be considered with regard to families and old people. When we used that argument to ask the government for amendments to the legislation authorizing payment of family allowances or pensions to the disabled and the old, we were laughed at.
It will be recalled that in 1945 when family allowances were established, the dollar and the cost of living were not what they are today. If it is fair to advocate a postal increase on the basis of a higher cost of living and
depreciation of the dollar, I ask the other ministers of the government, the Minister of Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) for instance, to invoke the same reason when a study is made of the legislation concerning family and welfare allowances, etc.
Mr. Speaker, if it is logical to consider such factors, it should have enabled ministers and members to provide for improvements in other fields that are as justified as the one we are asking for today.
Bill C-240 is a kind of little omnibus bill, which puts me in a somewhat conflicting position. As a matter of fact, it contains changes, two of which are necessary.
First, it provides for an increase in the commission to agents selling postage stamps. Indeed, I can understand that postmasters selling stamps to the public deserve a pay increase; after all, the pay they get from the Postmaster General is not always proportionate to the work they have to do. I can also understand that it could be very difficult for the minister responsible for the postal service and officials to establish standards that would be absolutely fair for all postmaster across this country. That is why whenever I happen to talk with postmasters who ask me to appeal to authoritiees in order to get them a pay increase, I always make it a point to find out the total number of their customers, their turnover, etc. so as to be sure that their request is justified.
Second, this bill provides for collective mailings free of postage in the case of members of Parliament. I believe I am justified in saying that I should support that provision had it been put forward separately.
A few weeks ago during the debate on Bill C-242, I pointed out to the government the needs of Parliament members for services and this service was precisely one of those, we wanted so as to have an additional tool to better serve the people.
I will not repeat what I have already asked and this is why, in my opinion, this is a kind of a small omnibus bill which contains both good and bad things. Therefore, we must determine whether the pros outweigh the cons.
This is why I have analyzed as objectively as possible all the provisions of the bill and taken it upon me to give my opinion during this debate.
I would like to conclude by asking the minister in charge of the Post Office when he closes this debate to enlighten the House about the printing of stamps. Are they still totally or partly printed by the British American Bank Note Company Limited? Are they still totally or partly printed by the Canadian Bank Note Company Lmited with all its equipment? Are they partly printed by the British American Bank Note Limited and partly by the Canadian Bank Note Company Limited? I would like the minister to tell the House why the printing of stamps is done by those two companies and what is the approximate annual amount paid to them, because, in the absence of information to the contrary, I always thought that the government did not buy the stamps sold to the public, but had them printed. In fact, I believed that the Queen's printer did the job, but according to the information obtained, it is entrusted to the two companies I have just mentioned.

I shall conclude with those remarks, since I consider them essential to the guidance of hon. members. I am convinced that the minister will in due course do his best to provide us with the information I am now requesting.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the passage of this bill but I have a few words to say about it.
Mr. Speaker, we are faced with an increase in postal rates which had been announced quite a while ago. We are aware of the fact that the Post Office is getting deeper and deeper into deficit and that it will keep sliding down unless something is done to correct the situation. According to the figures I have here, the Post Office deficit presently amounts to $113 million and it will get even worse in the years to come unless we regain control of the situation.
I wish to express my admiration for the minister who did everything he could and cannot be held responsible for these increases and for the problems facing the Post Office. The minister did a good job, with the means available to him, to correct quite a number of anomalous situations and we appreciate his work. For all he has done, we express our admiration, but much remains to be done.
Mr. Speaker, if postal services decrease and costs increase, there surely is something wrong somewhere. The people are getting less and less service. I shall not dwell on the subject at length for my colleagues have already spoken about it.
With regard to those services, I mailed letters in my riding that were delivered three weeks later. Like the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) I too asked for a report on the matter, and received good ones. I can only praise the postal employees who, in general, perform their duties well, but the mail took two or three weeks to cover a distance of roughly 300 miles. That is not normal. There is certainly something wrong. I blame the delay not on the carelessness of the minister but rather on certain civil servants who do not do their jobs properly, who do not take their responsibilities seriously where mail delivery is concerned.
But there are other responsibilities, of much greater significance, which are far from being properly assumed by civil servants, and this tends to increase operating costs and hence the cost of living generally. As for senior officials, I have something to say about them and I think I have already told the minister. Now I am not criticizing the minister, but I suggest he should consider straightening out the situation. Inquiries should be made because senior officials are terribly expensive to the Post Office.
Some officials are not discharging their responsibilities by a long shot. This I am saying quite frankly: they are wasting public money. I will give hon. members evidence of it, but without going into details for it would be too lengthy and would cause a public scandal.
In my riding, for instance, they first closed down the post office four years ago before building a new one. Floor space was rented elsewhere to house the post office. Since then, plans were made, tenders were called and withdrawn, in short, they changed their minds about seven or eight times. The fact remains that the post office building is closed. It could have been kept open to the public. Therefore, for the last three years, we have had to pay rent to house the post office elsewhere. It is terribly costly to the department and even if there were three or four sets of plans made and as many calls for tenders, none was accepted, all have been rejected to consider something else again.
That issue has been pending for three years now and has probably cost thousands of dollars to the department. It is not really the Post Office Department that is responsible, but the Department of Public Works, because the latter is responsible for the construction of buildings. Delays of this sort, for one reason or another, are inexcusable. Then, when information is asked for, one is told that bids will be called next week. This has been repeated for two years. One is told: They will be called next month; you can announce it in the newspapers, it is certain, the decisions have been made. But three years later, the decisions are still pending.
Therefore, I blame the civil servants who do this sort of thing, or the Department of Public Works, as this increases the operating cost of the postal service. We are debating today a proposal for an increase in the postal rates because of all sorts of things of this nature. I could say a lot more on the subject.
I know many other things, but I shall not say more tonight. I would not want a public scandal.
All kinds of factors contribute to increase postal rates and hence the cost of living. And this is done everywhere. If it is done on a national scale in Canada, you can imagine how much it costs.
So, I ask the minister to work in co-operation with the Department of Public Works responsible for the construction of post offices. So the minister can certainly act, and ask for investigations. There are certainly some way to save, so that the people will pay reasonable rates. I repeat that senior officials are not serious, and do not fulfill their duty as they should, that is honestly and fairly. I do not condemn in any way the minister for this increase of postal rates.
As a conclusion to my remarks, I shall not go into details, because many other speakers have done so. I only meant to ask the minister to conduct serious investigations so that these abuses may end some day, that we may have more justice, and that the department might

June 1, 1971

offer a reasonable postal rate. It is desirable that services be paid for as long as there are no abuses. It is possible to find some solutions to this problem so that the minister might save as much public money as possible. The public can then expect better services, because if it is possible to reduce expenses, better services can be provided even though the Post Office Department should not be considered a national bank or the Bank of Canada.
Before closing I would like to say how much I admire the minister because he does his work well. I obtained answers to all my requests, and was given all kinds of assurances. He told me the truth and I admire him for it. He is fair and we can trust his word. He is not to blame for mistakes or nonsense which originate in other quarters. I ask him once again, with all due respect to him and the government, to do us justice, because it is not easy to understand some of the things that are happening.

He should make that magazine pay more lor bothering the Canadian people with stuff they do not ask for and do not want. The magazine sends out second, third and fourth reminders. We want the minister to say, "We will put up your mailing rate and make you pay whatever it costs the Post Office Department to handle all the junk that you send out." If the minister wants us to stop talking and allow him to get the floor and close the debate before ten o'clock, we will not do it, Mr. Speaker.
Mailing rates are to increase another cent for first-class mail on July 1 and another cent on January 1 next, bringing the rate up to eight cents. The rates for these magazines will not go up, yet each day they take up the time of the post office and the time of the community. The effort put out by the Post Office Department on these magazines is far out of proportion to what they are entitled to when one considers what they do.
I wish to cite another example. I recall that a publication was put out by the metropolitan Toronto policemen's association. It was a mimeographed, monthly newsletter, Mr. Speaker, and the association used to spend between $300 and $500 a year on postage. Their rate has now gone up by 400 per cent, so they do not send out the publication any more. Here was a perfectly legitimate, non-profit communication sent to a group of Canadian citizens who belonged to the association as a result of their occupation, and the minister "upped" their mailing bill. He did not "up" the mailing bill for Time and Reader's Digest. Those magazines must be candidates for social welfare because the Post Office Department still lets them get away with murder.
Unless the minister can come up with similar exemptions for publications such as I have mentioned, and until the treasury can pick up the deficit resulting from the imbalance in mail as between the United States and Canada, he need not ask us to hold still while he seeks to increase first-class postal rates. If you divide two into 42 you get 21. If old age pensioners send 21 additional letters, that will take up the 42 cents the government gave them when it increased the basic old age pension. How can the minister expect us to listen and wait with bated breath while he increases the first-class mailing rate? Until we have an assurance that the minister will say something about the items which have been mentioned, and until we have an assurance that he will deal with them seriously, we will hold up this bill.

Mr. Speaker, the record will show that I have been attempting for many months to obtain a full and satisfactory answer from the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on the question of an outstanding CMHC mortgage on Rochdale College in Toronto. In fairness to the minister involved I have taken into account the fact that during that period there were extenuating circumstances in the Rochdale account which have tended to complicate the matter. There is the fact that Rochdale masquerades as an educational institution and these institutions normally receive preferential or at least less rigid treatment from lending institutions.
However, the complications in the Rochdale account have been due largely to the attitude of the minister rather than to any points of law or any regulations with regard to amortization of CMHC loans. I submit to the minister that if the Rochdale loan had been made to me instead of to the college, the loan would have been foreclosed many months ago, the Canadian people would have their money back and they would have a building to cover the defaulted principal and interest payments.
I have watched the proceedings with respect to the Rochdale College loan over a period of many months and am deeply concerned over the way in which a loan of such magnitude has been permitted to fall 14 months in arrears. I am concerned that the minister has of his own will and accord chosen to view Rochdale College in a way that is inconsistent with the regulations under which CMHC is required to operate and totally inconsistent with sound business and management practices. If all Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages were serviced in a like manner it would not take long for an overactive imagination to conjure up a vision of complete and utter chaos in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation operations.

June 1, 1971

By way of background I would like to read into the record-the specific figures of the Rochdale College mortgage. The approved loan was in the amount of $4,884,165.90, a princely sum of money to risk on an experimental educational project to be run by its own students. The interest rate on the loan was very attractive at 51 per cent per annum. As of April 30 this year the loan was in default by 14 months for a total of $359,853.37. During all my years in business I have neither seen nor heard of anything quite like it. I therefore feel justified in asking for a full explanation of this apparent disregard for the sanctity of the public purse.
Hear, hear!

One of my reasons for indulging in the past the minister's reluctance to answer my questions is that Rochdale is called a college and as such has been wearing a mantle of respectability that is totally undeserved. I have been, and am now, prepared to bend a little to accommodate educational institutions, but it has been evident for some time that Rochdale has been sailing under false colours. Almost from the day it opened, Rochdale College has been the symbol of everything that is wrong in our society. In the files of the Toronto police department there is evidence that Rochdale rivals Yorkville village as a haven for drug users and pushers, hippies and yippies, deviates and social misfits of every type and description.
There are recorded cases of underage, runaway children being lured into Rochdale and kept there for the depraved satisfaction of so-called students some of whom are as much as 35 years of age. By way of further clarification, to qualify as a student at this so-called college simply means that you can afford to pay the $80 per month single, or $50 double occupancy rate. There are no course requirements, no attendance requirements, no professors and no system of examination or grading.
I would like to make just a couple of brief, additional observations before I conclude. The first concerns an item in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 21, 1971, wherein it was stated that Rochdale College accepts welfare cases from the city welfare department, some of them families with small children. I ask my hon. colleagues in this House, does this sound like a college? In days gone by it would have been called a flop-house and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, or any other government agency would have laughed at the thought of supporting such an institution with public funds. A few days ago the Toronto police department raided Rochdale College-not for the first time-and confiscated a quantity of marijuana, hashish and chemical drugs while arresting three students. As the police left the college they were pelted with eggs and refuse and subjected to verbal abuse.
In conclusion, I would like to assure the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that I am not asking him to assume the role of protector of public or private morality. However, I do expect the minister to exercise proper judgment in deciding who qualifies for Central Mortgage and Housing Cor-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion poration mortgages. Rochdale College is a rabbit warren where anything goes, and the more anti-social and uncivilized the better. I call upon the minister responsible for the Rochdale mortgage to recover the money involved and to put it back into the public coffers where some better use for it can be found.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in August, 1966, a loan of $4,844,165 was made to Co-operative College Residences Incorporated to assist in the construction of a students' residence, now known as Rochdale College, on Bloor Street in Toronto. The administration of Rochdale College has experienced great difficulty in generating sufficient revenues to pay all the operating costs of the building, including the National Housing Act mortgage. Up to the present time arrears in mortgage payments have accumulated to the extent of $340,000.
If the problem of Rochdale College were simply a mortgage problem, the solution itself would be a straightforward matter, involving action by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to recover the public investment in Rochdale and to assume responsibility for the management of the building. The problem of Rochdale College involves considerations other than a mortgage in arrears.
While many of the negative aspects of its administration have received the greatest attention, some of the more positive aspects of their program have not been established or understood, including the role that Rochdale plays in the lives of many young people in metropolitan Toronto. There are, therefore, both social and financial implications to consider in dealing with Rochdale College.
Nearly two months ago an interdepartmental committee was formed at the request of the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to consider and assess alternative courses of action by which the public investment in Rochdale may be protected. The committee is under the chairmanship of the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and includes representatives of the Privy Council office, the Department of National Health and Welfare, Secretary of State, Solicitor General and the Department of Finance.
In carrying out its work, the committee is considering all aspects of the Rochdale situation and in addition to the interested departments of the federal government the committee has met the council of Rochdale, representatives of the metropolitan Toronto corporation, the city of Toronto and departments and agencies of the Ontario provincial government. It is expected that the committee will report its findings through the responsible minister shortly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister without Portfolio in charge of citi-

June 1, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion zenship programs (Mr. Stanbury) the following question, as reported as page 6207 of Hansard:
In view of the large numbers of young people now travelling In Canada, is the government considering a program to provide capital assistance for youth hostel facilities?
I went on to explain that I asked this question owing to the fact that the current program is restricted to operational assistance. I was very much surprised when the minister answered my question in three words, namely, "No, Mr. Speaker". I should like briefly to review some of the factors involved in this brief exchange.
Over the last two or three years there has been a very sharp increase in the number of young people travelling across Canada and using a variety of means of unconventional travel, one might say. In particular, many young people are hitch-hiking their way across the country during the summer months, in this way seeing their country. One of the reasons they have taken to the roads is that they have a great deal of difficulty obtaining any sort of suitable employment, indeed any sort of employment at all in many cases.
Last year the government responded with its program of assistance for facilities for overnight accommodation for many of these travelling young people. This was of tremendous assistance for the most part. I understand use was made of government facilities such as armouries. This year a somewhat different tactic was adopted in respect of this program. A program was established to provide assistance to various communities and groups but the government decided to rely more heavily on local community initiative in the establishment of various facilities providing accommodation for young, travelling people.
One feature of the grants provided by the federal government under this youth hostel program is, as I indicated earlier-I refer now to a government statement issued by the department which was kindly supplied to me-that grants can cover salaries and operating expenses but cannot cover capital expenditures. That is a flat prohibition in respect of assistance for capital expenditures.
The reason I asked this question was not because I had any expectation the government had a program ready to announce yesterday, today or tomorrow, but because it seemed to me perfectly reasonable to expect that the department would now have looked at this problem from a long-range point of view. It is obvious that this new phenomenon is going to continue. It will be with us for some time and the department should be looking at it from a longer-range point of view.
I also want to make it clear that I am not suggesting we have to rely entirely or even primarily on government assistance or initiative for the establishment of permanent facilities for travelling young people. It seems to me the government does have some responsibility and could provide a very useful service if it took the initiative now in studying this matter and carrying on discussions with interested groups and people in order to arrive
at a method whereby the federal government could provide assistance and encouragement to groups and communities who wish to establish permanent facilities and accommodation for young people who are travelling, particularly during the summer months.
I hope the minister will indicate tonight that his department intends to look at this matter with a view to developing some means to encourage discussion among communities across Canada and the development of means to provide stimulus for and encouragement of community efforts in the provision of satisfactory facilities.
I also asked a supplementary question concerning alternative means of assistance this year toward the provision of facilities in communities where difficulties have been encountered in obtaining approval from municipal authorities. The minister indicated there are a number of ways in which assistance can be provided to communities in this regard. I hope the department and the minister will take advantage of every possible opportunity to encourage communities to provide these facilities, and that they will in fact develop other possible means of communication with communities across Canada in order to arrive at satisfactory arrangements. I include MPs in this category.
I draw to the minister's attention that my colleague, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin), and myself issued a statement last week in which we indicated our unhappiness with certain developments in the city of Regina regarding a planned program there. Unfortunately, with regard to my own city the council saw fit to react on a short-term basis, with a short-run view of the situation in response to a request regarding the establishment of a local hostel. It seems to me that a little leadership by the council and interested parties could have been given to overcome the fears of the local citizens. In this way a satisfactory program might have been established which would in fact have benefited these young people. This could have been a credit to the city of Regina and Canada as a whole.
Thus, I hope the minister will look at these programs in terms of continuing the assistance undertaken over the past couple of years. I hope he will take a long-range view of this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for raising this matter which is of considerable concern to me and to the citizenship branch. As the hon. member mentioned, last year the federal government for the first time undertook to assist communities to cope with the presence of transient youth and also to help young people travelling across our country find accommodation wherever they might be. This year we have doubled the budget for that kind of assistance, but we do not yet feel we have enough funds or enough information to launch a program of capital assistance. I hope, as I think the hon. member does, that some day Canada will have a national system of hostels, although not necessarily sponsored by the government. I hope, rather, that it would be in the hands of voluntary organizations as I believe is usually the case in European countries.

June 1, 1971

I feel, however, that those Canadians who seem to jealously guard the boundaries of their cities against the alien hordes of other young Canadians for elsewhere in Canada seem sometimes to have a sort of double standard. Very often these are the same people who are proudly sending off their own spunky children to hike about Europe.

It has been our experience that the successful operation of a youth hostel or other service to travelling young people is in large measure dependent upon the attitude of the local community. For this reason our summer hostel program this year is one of response to local initiatives and one which attempts to involve as broad as possible a range of community groups. Naturally, we are interested in the attitude of the municipal
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion councils although this is not the only criterion on which community initiatives can be judged. Through our regional offices we try to maintain close liaison with voluntary groups and municipal and provincial authorities in assessing local needs and developing our response to them.
We want to assist in every way possible in responding to the requests of local authorities and voluntary organizations. We are prepared to do that in Regina as elsewhere. I hope the people of Regina and their elected representatives will be able to make arrangements to accommodate the young Canadians who will be in Regina this summer, as other communities are doing in other parts of Canada.
